requirements.text: Limit system access to authorized users, processes acting on behalf of authorized users, and devices (including other systems).
requirements.plainEnglish: Only the people, programs, and devices you have approved should be able to get into your systems. Keep a list of who and what is allowed. Turn off access for anyone or anything not on that list.
requirements.whyItMatters: If you don't know who can get in, you can't protect what's inside. Most other controls depend on first knowing who is allowed to use your systems.
examples: Every employee signs in with their own named account. No shared logins.
A list of company laptops and phones that are allowed to connect to company email and files.
Accounts for people who have left the company are disabled on their last day.
evidence: List of authorized users and their accounts
List of authorized devices
Account management procedure (how accounts are requested, approved, and removed)
Screenshots of user lists from your systems (for example, Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace admin)

requirements.text: Limit system access to the types of transactions and functions that authorized users are permitted to execute.
requirements.plainEnglish: Once someone is signed in, they should only be able to do what their job needs. A bookkeeper doesn't need admin rights. A field technician doesn't need access to payroll.
requirements.whyItMatters: Limiting what each account can do reduces the damage from mistakes, insider misuse, or a stolen password.
examples: Only two people have administrator rights in your email system.
Shared folders containing contract files are restricted to the project team.
Regular user accounts cannot install software.
evidence: Roles or groups and the permissions each one has
Access control policy
Screenshots of folder or application permissions

requirements.text: Control the flow of CUI in accordance with approved authorizations.
requirements.plainEnglish: Decide where CUI is allowed to go, and set up your systems so it can only go there. For example, you might share CUI with your prime contractor through an approved portal. It should not be emailed to personal accounts or uploaded to unapproved cloud storage.
requirements.whyItMatters: CUI often leaks by being sent somewhere it shouldn't go, not by being stolen. Controlling where it can flow keeps it inside the places you protect.
examples: Email rules that block or warn when CUI-labeled messages are sent outside the company.
Company files can only sync to the approved cloud storage, not to personal accounts.
A firewall that only allows traffic to and from approved destinations.
evidence: Data handling or information flow policy
Diagram showing where CUI is stored and where it is allowed to go
Firewall, email, or data loss prevention (DLP) settings that enforce those limits

requirements.text: Separate the duties of individuals to reduce the risk of malevolent activity without collusion.
requirements.plainEnglish: Split up important tasks so one person can't do something harmful alone. For example, the person who approves new accounts shouldn't be the only one who creates them. In a very small company, a second person reviewing the work can serve the same purpose.
requirements.whyItMatters: When key tasks need two people, it's much harder for one person to cause damage, by mistake or on purpose, without someone noticing.
examples: A manager approves account requests, and IT sets them up.
An outside IT provider administers systems, and the owner reviews reports of admin activity.
A second person reviews changes to firewall rules before they are made.
evidence: List of key duties and who performs each one
Separation of duties policy or procedure
Role assignments in your systems that match the documented split

requirements.text: Employ the principle of least privilege, including for specific security functions and privileged accounts.
requirements.plainEnglish: Give each person and account only the access needed for their job, and nothing more. This matters most for admin accounts and for security settings.
requirements.whyItMatters: The less access each account has, the less damage a mistake, a misuse, or a stolen password can cause.
examples: Staff use standard accounts. Only IT has admin rights.
Only one or two named people can change security settings in your email system.
Access is reviewed regularly and removed when no longer needed.
evidence: List of admin (privileged) accounts and who holds them
Records of regular access reviews
Access control policy describing least privilege

requirements.text: Use non-privileged accounts or roles when accessing nonsecurity functions.
requirements.plainEnglish: People with admin rights should also have a regular account and use it for everyday work like email and web browsing. They sign in with the admin account only for admin tasks.
requirements.whyItMatters: If an admin opens a malicious email while signed in as admin, the attacker gets admin powers. Using a regular account for daily work limits that risk.
examples: Your IT person has two accounts: one for daily work and a separate one for admin tasks.
Admin accounts have no mailbox and are not used to browse the web.
evidence: List of admin users and their separate everyday accounts
Policy requiring regular accounts for everyday work

requirements.text: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions and capture the execution of such functions in audit logs.
requirements.plainEnglish: Regular users should not be able to do admin-level things, like installing software, changing security settings, or turning off antivirus. When admin actions do happen, your systems should record them in logs.
requirements.whyItMatters: Blocking admin actions for regular users stops many attacks. Logging the admin actions that do happen lets you spot misuse and investigate problems.
examples: Regular users can't install software or change system settings on company computers.
Admin sign-ins and admin changes are recorded in the audit logs of your email and device management systems.
evidence: Settings showing that standard users don't have admin rights
Audit logging settings
Sample log entries showing admin actions being recorded

requirements.text: Limit unsuccessful logon attempts.
requirements.plainEnglish: After several wrong passwords in a row, lock the account for a while or until someone unlocks it. Choose the number of attempts and the lockout time, write them down, and set your systems to enforce them.
requirements.whyItMatters: Attackers often try password after password until one works. Lockouts stop that kind of guessing.
examples: Accounts lock for 15 minutes after 5 failed sign-in attempts.
Your cloud email system blocks sign-ins after repeated failures.
evidence: Account lockout policy stating the number of attempts and the lockout time
Screenshots of lockout settings in your systems

requirements.text: Provide privacy and security notices consistent with applicable CUI rules.
requirements.plainEnglish: Show a notice when people sign in to systems that handle CUI. It tells users the system is for authorized use only, that activity may be monitored, and anything else your CUI rules require.
requirements.whyItMatters: The notice reminds users of their responsibilities and makes the rules clear to anyone who uses the system.
examples: A sign-in banner on company computers saying the system is for authorized business use and may be monitored.
The same notice on the sign-in page for remote access.
evidence: The text of your notice
Screenshots of the notice shown at sign-in

requirements.text: Use session lock with pattern-hiding displays to prevent access and viewing of data after a period of inactivity.
requirements.plainEnglish: If a computer sits unused for a set time, lock the screen and hide what was on it. The user must sign in again to get back in.
requirements.whyItMatters: An unlocked, unattended screen lets anyone walking by see CUI or use the account.
examples: Company computers lock after 15 minutes of inactivity and show a lock screen instead of open documents.
Company phones lock automatically after a short idle time.
evidence: Screen lock policy stating the time limit
Device management or group policy settings that enforce it

requirements.text: Terminate (automatically) a user session after a defined condition.
requirements.plainEnglish: Sign users out automatically when certain conditions are met, such as a long period of inactivity or a maximum session length. Decide which conditions apply and set your systems to enforce them.
requirements.whyItMatters: Sessions left open indefinitely can be picked up and misused by someone else.
examples: Web applications sign users out after 8 hours.
Remote access sessions disconnect after 30 minutes of inactivity.
evidence: Documented conditions that end a session
Screenshots of session timeout settings

requirements.text: Monitor and control remote access sessions.
requirements.plainEnglish: Keep track of who connects to your systems from outside the office, and be able to control or cut off those connections. Remote access includes VPNs (secure connections into the company network), remote desktop, and remote support tools.
requirements.whyItMatters: Remote access is a common way in for attackers. Watching and controlling it helps you notice and stop connections that shouldn't be there.
examples: VPN connection logs are kept and reviewed.
Remote support tools require the user to approve each session.
Remote access for an account can be turned off immediately when needed.
evidence: Remote access policy
List of approved remote access methods
Sample remote access logs

requirements.text: Employ cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of remote access sessions.
requirements.plainEnglish: Encrypt remote connections so no one can read the data as it travels over the internet. Most modern VPNs and remote access tools can do this. Confirm yours does and that it's turned on. When encryption protects CUI, it generally needs to be FIPS-validated, meaning tested and approved under a U.S. government standard. Requirement 3.13.11 covers this.
requirements.whyItMatters: Unencrypted connections can be intercepted, exposing CUI and passwords.
examples: Staff connect through a VPN that uses FIPS-validated encryption.
Remote desktop is only allowed over an encrypted connection.
evidence: Remote access settings showing encryption is on
Vendor documentation showing the encryption is FIPS-validated

requirements.text: Route remote access via managed access control points.
requirements.plainEnglish: Send all remote connections through a few approved entry points that you manage, such as one company VPN. Don't let people connect directly to individual computers from outside.
requirements.whyItMatters: A few managed entry points are easier to protect and monitor than many scattered ones.
examples: All remote access goes through the company VPN or a single remote access gateway.
Direct remote desktop connections from the internet to office computers are blocked.
evidence: Network diagram showing the remote access entry points
Firewall rules that block other remote access paths

requirements.text: Authorize remote execution of privileged commands and remote access to security-relevant information.
requirements.plainEnglish: Decide in advance who may do admin tasks remotely, and who may remotely view security information such as logs and security settings. Allow only those approved people.
requirements.whyItMatters: Remote admin access is powerful. Limiting it to approved people reduces the chance it's misused.
examples: Only your IT provider's named technicians may administer systems remotely.
Remote admin access is approved and documented before it's set up.
evidence: List of people approved for remote admin access
Approval records or policy
Settings that limit remote admin access to those people

requirements.text: Authorize wireless access prior to allowing such connections.
requirements.plainEnglish: Approve Wi-Fi access before anyone uses it to connect to your systems. Decide which wireless networks are allowed and how devices may connect to them.
requirements.whyItMatters: Unapproved wireless connections can let outsiders onto your network.
examples: Only the company Wi-Fi network is approved for company devices in the office.
Visitors use a separate guest Wi-Fi with no access to company systems.
evidence: Wireless access policy
List of approved wireless networks and their settings

requirements.text: Protect wireless access using authentication and encryption.
requirements.plainEnglish: Protect your Wi-Fi with a strong sign-in method and encryption. Only approved people and devices should be able to connect, and nobody else should be able to read the traffic.
requirements.whyItMatters: Open or weakly protected Wi-Fi can be joined or listened in on from outside the building.
examples: The office Wi-Fi uses WPA2-Enterprise or WPA3, the strongest security settings on most Wi-Fi equipment.
The Wi-Fi password is strong and is changed when someone leaves the company.
evidence: Wireless router or access point settings showing the sign-in method and encryption
Wireless access policy

requirements.text: Control connection of mobile devices.
requirements.plainEnglish: Decide which phones, tablets, and laptops may connect to your systems, and under what conditions. Enforce those rules, for example with a mobile device management (MDM) tool.
requirements.whyItMatters: Uncontrolled mobile devices can carry CUI out of your protected systems or bring in malware.
examples: Only company-managed phones can access company email.
Devices must have a passcode and current updates before they can connect.
evidence: Mobile device policy
Device management settings and a list of enrolled devices

requirements.text: Encrypt CUI on mobile devices and mobile computing platforms.
requirements.plainEnglish: Turn on encryption for laptops, phones, and tablets that store CUI, so the data can't be read if the device is lost or stolen. When encryption protects CUI, it generally needs to be FIPS-validated, meaning tested and approved under a U.S. government standard. Requirement 3.13.11 covers this.
requirements.whyItMatters: Mobile devices are easily lost or stolen. Encryption keeps the data on them unreadable to whoever ends up with the device.
examples: Full-disk encryption, such as BitLocker or FileVault, is on for all company laptops.
Company phones are encrypted and require a passcode.
evidence: Device management report showing encryption status for each device
Encryption policy

requirements.text: Verify and control/limit connections to and use of external systems.
requirements.plainEnglish: External systems are ones you don't own or control, like personal computers, a customer's network, or a third-party service. Decide whether and how they may connect to your systems or handle your CUI, and enforce those limits.
requirements.whyItMatters: You can't vouch for the security of systems you don't control. Limiting their use keeps CUI from ending up somewhere unprotected.
examples: Employees may not use personal computers to access CUI.
Cloud services must be approved before use, and only approved services may store CUI.
evidence: Policy on using external systems
List of approved external systems and services
Agreements with service providers

requirements.text: Limit use of portable storage devices on external systems.
requirements.plainEnglish: Limit how company USB drives and other portable storage are used on computers you don't control. Examples are a customer's computer or a home computer.
requirements.whyItMatters: Plugging company storage into an unknown computer can expose CUI or bring malware back into your company.
examples: Company USB drives may only be used on company computers.
Using portable storage on outside computers requires approval.
evidence: Portable storage policy
Device control settings, if you use them

requirements.text: Control CUI posted or processed on publicly accessible systems.
requirements.plainEnglish: Make sure CUI never ends up on public systems like your website or public social media. Decide who may post content, and review content before it goes public.
requirements.whyItMatters: Once CUI is posted publicly, anyone can copy it, and it can't be taken back.
examples: Only two named people can publish to the company website.
Content is checked for CUI before it's posted.
Public content is reviewed regularly, and any CUI found is removed.
evidence: List of people authorized to post public content
Procedure for reviewing content before posting
Records of those reviews

requirements.text: Ensure that managers, systems administrators, and users of organizational systems are made aware of the security risks associated with their activities and of the applicable policies, standards, and procedures related to the security of those systems.
requirements.plainEnglish: Make sure everyone who uses your systems, including managers and whoever runs your IT, knows the security risks that come with their work. They also need to know your security policies and procedures. Usually this means security awareness training when people start and regularly after that.
requirements.whyItMatters: Many security problems start with a person clicking a bad link, sharing a password, or not knowing a rule. People can't follow rules they've never been told.
examples: New employees complete security awareness training in their first week, covering phishing, passwords, and handling CUI.
Everyone repeats the training each year and signs that they've read the security policies.
Short reminders about current scams are shared at staff meetings.
evidence: Security awareness training materials
Training records showing who completed training and when
Signed acknowledgments of your security policies

requirements.text: Ensure that personnel are trained to carry out their assigned information security-related duties and responsibilities.
requirements.plainEnglish: People with security jobs need training for those jobs. First, write down who is responsible for which security tasks, such as managing accounts, reviewing logs, or handling backups. Then make sure each person is trained to do their tasks.
requirements.whyItMatters: Security tasks done by someone who doesn't know how to do them often aren't done properly. Clear assignments also make sure no task falls through the cracks.
examples: A list of security roles shows that the office manager handles user accounts and the IT provider manages the firewall.
The person who manages accounts completed the vendor's training for the admin console.
When an outside IT provider holds a security role, the qualifications of their staff are checked.
evidence: List of security roles and responsibilities, and who holds each one
Training records or certificates for the people in those roles
Contract terms covering the qualifications of outside IT providers

requirements.text: Provide security awareness training on recognizing and reporting potential indicators of insider threat.
requirements.plainEnglish: An insider threat is a risk from someone who already has access, such as an employee or contractor. They might misuse that access on purpose or by mistake. Teach managers and employees to notice and report the warning signs, and tell them who to report to. Warning signs include asking for access they don't need, copying large amounts of data, or repeatedly ignoring security rules.
requirements.whyItMatters: People inside the company already have access, so the usual defenses may not stop them. Coworkers are often the first to notice something is wrong.
examples: Annual security training includes a section on insider threat warning signs and how to report concerns.
Employees know they can report concerns confidentially to a named manager.
evidence: Insider threat training materials
Training records showing managers and employees completed it
The documented way to report concerns

requirements.text: Create and retain system audit logs and records to the extent needed to enable the monitoring, analysis, investigation, and reporting of unlawful or unauthorized system activity.
requirements.plainEnglish: Turn on logging in your systems so they record important events, such as sign-ins, failed sign-ins, admin changes, and access to CUI. Decide which events to log and what each log entry must include. Keep the logs for a set period of time.
requirements.whyItMatters: Without logs, you can't tell what happened during a security incident, who did it, or when. Logs are often the only evidence.
examples: Audit logging is turned on in your email and file sharing system, such as Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace.
Computers and the firewall send their logs to one central place.
Logs are kept for one year, as set in your logging policy.
evidence: Logging policy listing the events to log, what each entry contains, and how long logs are kept
Screenshots of audit logging settings
Sample log entries

requirements.text: Ensure that the actions of individual system users can be uniquely traced to those users, so they can be held accountable for their actions.
requirements.plainEnglish: Make sure every action in your logs can be tied to one specific person. That means everyone uses their own account, and the logs record which account did what.
requirements.whyItMatters: If several people share an account, a log entry can't show who did something, so no one can be held accountable.
examples: No shared logins: each person signs in with their own named account.
Log entries include the username, the time, and what was done.
evidence: Policy banning shared accounts
Sample log entries showing individual usernames
User account list showing each account belongs to one person

requirements.text: Review and update logged events.
requirements.plainEnglish: Every so often, review which events your systems log, and change the list when needed. For example, start logging a system you've just added, or stop logging events that turned out to be useless. Decide how often you'll do this review.
requirements.whyItMatters: Your systems and risks change over time. A logging setup that never gets reviewed slowly stops capturing the events that matter.
examples: Logged events are reviewed once a year and whenever a new system is added.
After a security scare, logging was added for file downloads from the shared drive.
evidence: Documented schedule for reviewing logged events
Records of past reviews and the changes made

requirements.text: Alert in the event of an audit logging process failure.
requirements.plainEnglish: Set up an alert so the right person finds out if logging stops working. For example, log storage might fill up or the logging service might stop. Decide who gets the alert and which failures trigger it.
requirements.whyItMatters: If logging stops without anyone noticing, you lose the record of what's happening, and you may not find out until you need it.
examples: The log system emails the IT provider if it stops receiving logs.
An alert is sent when log storage is almost full.
evidence: Alert settings for logging failures
List of who receives the alerts
A sample alert

requirements.text: Correlate audit record review, analysis, and reporting processes for investigation and response to indications of unlawful, unauthorized, suspicious, or unusual activity.
requirements.plainEnglish: When you investigate suspicious activity, look at the logs from different systems together, not one at a time. For example, compare email sign-in logs with remote access (VPN) logs and computer logs to piece together what happened. Write down how you review, analyze, and report on logs.
requirements.whyItMatters: An attack often leaves small traces in several systems. Looking at them together shows the full picture.
examples: Logs from email, computers, and the firewall are collected in one tool so they can be searched together.
A written procedure explains how suspicious activity in the logs is investigated and reported.
evidence: Log review and investigation procedure
Settings showing logs from several systems collected in one place
Records of past log reviews

requirements.text: Provide audit record reduction and report generation to support on-demand analysis and reporting.
requirements.plainEnglish: Have tools that can filter large amounts of log data down to what matters and produce reports when you need them. Most cloud services and logging tools have built-in search and reporting that can do this.
requirements.whyItMatters: Logs are huge. Without a way to search and summarize them, they're nearly useless when you need answers quickly.
examples: The admin console can search sign-in logs by user and date and export a report.
A monthly report of failed sign-ins and admin changes is produced from the logging tool.
evidence: Screenshots of log search and reporting features
Sample log reports

requirements.text: Provide a system capability that compares and synchronizes internal system clocks with an authoritative source to generate time stamps for audit records.
requirements.plainEnglish: Make sure all your systems set their clocks automatically from the same trusted time source. That way the times in your logs are accurate and match across systems.
requirements.whyItMatters: If clocks disagree, you can't line up events from different systems during an investigation.
examples: Company computers get their time from an official internet time service or the company server.
Cloud services use their provider's synchronized time.
evidence: Time settings showing the time source each system uses
Documentation naming your trusted time source

requirements.text: Protect audit information and audit logging tools from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion.
requirements.plainEnglish: Protect logs and logging tools so no one can read, change, or delete them without permission. That includes people who might want to cover their tracks.
requirements.whyItMatters: An attacker or insider who can edit or erase logs can hide what they did.
examples: Only a few named admins can view or manage logs.
Logs are copied to a separate system that regular users and most admins can't change.
Deleting logs is turned off or requires special approval.
evidence: Permission settings for logs and logging tools
List of people with access to logs
Log storage settings showing logs are protected from changes and deletion

requirements.text: Limit management of audit logging functionality to a subset of privileged users.
requirements.plainEnglish: Only a small, named group of admins should be able to change logging settings, such as turning logging off or changing what's logged. Not every admin needs this power.
requirements.whyItMatters: The fewer people who control logging, the less chance it gets turned off by mistake or to hide something.
examples: Only the IT manager can change audit logging settings in the email system.
Other admins can view logs but can't change logging settings.
evidence: List of people allowed to manage logging
Role settings showing only those people have that permission

requirements.text: Establish and maintain baseline configurations and inventories of organizational systems (including hardware, software, firmware, and documentation) throughout the respective system development life cycles.
requirements.plainEnglish: Keep an up-to-date list of your equipment and software. Also write down the standard setup for each kind of system, such as how a company laptop is configured. This standard setup is called a baseline configuration. Update both whenever things change.
requirements.whyItMatters: You can't protect what you don't know you have. A written standard setup makes it easy to spot systems that have drifted from it.
examples: An inventory lists every laptop, phone, server, network device, and software subscription, with its owner.
A document describes the standard laptop setup: operating system version, required software, and security settings.
The inventory is reviewed every quarter and whenever equipment is bought or retired.
evidence: Hardware and software inventory
Baseline configuration documents
Records showing the inventory and baselines are reviewed and updated

requirements.text: Establish and enforce security configuration settings for information technology products employed in organizational systems.
requirements.plainEnglish: Choose secure settings for your computers, phones, network equipment, and software, and make sure they stay that way. Published security checklists from vendors or government sources are a good starting point.
requirements.whyItMatters: Many products come with settings that favor convenience over security. Attackers look for those weak defaults.
examples: Company laptops get a security settings checklist, such as the vendor's recommended security baseline, applied through device management.
Default passwords on the router and printers are changed.
Device management reports flag laptops whose settings no longer match.
evidence: Documented security settings for each type of system
Device management or group policy settings that enforce them
Reports showing devices meet the settings

requirements.text: Track, review, approve or disapprove, and log changes to organizational systems.
requirements.plainEnglish: Keep track of changes to your systems, such as new software, setting changes, or new equipment. Review each change and approve or reject it before it's made, and keep a record.
requirements.whyItMatters: Unplanned changes can break things or open security holes. A record of changes also helps you work out what went wrong.
examples: Changes are requested by email or ticket and approved by the owner or IT manager.
A simple change log records what changed, when, who made the change, and who approved it.
evidence: Change management procedure
Change log or tickets showing review and approval

requirements.text: Analyze the security impact of changes prior to implementation.
requirements.plainEnglish: Before making a change, think through how it could affect security. For example, ask whether a new app needs access to CUI, or whether a firewall change opens your network more than it should.
requirements.whyItMatters: Changes made without thinking about security are a common source of new weaknesses.
examples: The change request form asks how the change affects security.
Before a new cloud app was approved, someone checked how it stores data.
evidence: Change requests showing the security impact was considered
Change management procedure that requires a security review

requirements.text: Define, document, approve, and enforce physical and logical access restrictions associated with changes to organizational systems.
requirements.plainEnglish: Decide who may make changes to your systems, both physically (like opening the network closet) and electronically (like changing settings). Write the rules down, have them approved, and enforce them.
requirements.whyItMatters: If anyone can change systems, mistakes and unauthorized changes are much more likely.
examples: Only the IT provider and the office manager have keys to the network closet.
Only admin accounts can install software or change system settings.
The owner approves the list of people who may make changes.
evidence: Approved list of who may make physical and electronic changes
Settings showing only those people have permission to make changes
Records of who has keys or badge access to equipment rooms

requirements.text: Employ the principle of least functionality by configuring organizational systems to provide only essential capabilities.
requirements.plainEnglish: Set up each system to do only what it's needed for, and turn off everything else. For example, a computer used for office work doesn't need to run a web server.
requirements.whyItMatters: Every extra feature or service is one more thing an attacker could exploit.
examples: Unneeded features and apps are removed from company laptops.
The office server runs only the file sharing service it's used for.
evidence: List of the functions each type of system needs
Configuration settings showing other functions are turned off

requirements.text: Restrict, disable, or prevent the use of nonessential programs, functions, ports, protocols, and services.
requirements.plainEnglish: Work out which programs, features, network ports, protocols, and services your systems actually need, and block or turn off the rest. Ports and protocols are the channels systems use to talk to each other over a network.
requirements.whyItMatters: Unneeded programs and open network channels give attackers more ways in.
examples: The firewall blocks all incoming connections except the few that are needed.
Outdated file sharing protocols are turned off on company computers.
Games and other unneeded programs are removed from company devices.
evidence: List of allowed programs, ports, protocols, and services
Firewall rules
Configuration settings showing everything else is turned off

requirements.text: Apply deny-by-exception (blacklisting) policy to prevent the use of unauthorized software or deny-all, permit-by-exception (whitelisting) policy to allow the execution of authorized software.
requirements.plainEnglish: Control which software can run on your systems in one of two ways. You can block a list of software you don't allow. Or, more securely, you can allow only a list of approved software and block everything else. Decide which approach you use and keep the list up to date.
requirements.whyItMatters: Stopping unapproved software from running blocks a lot of malware and risky programs.
examples: Device management allows only approved apps to install and run on company laptops.
A list of banned software is blocked through your antivirus or device management tool.
evidence: Policy stating whether you allow only approved software or block specific software
The list of approved or blocked software
Settings in the tool that enforces the list

requirements.text: Control and monitor user-installed software.
requirements.plainEnglish: Set a rule about whether employees may install software themselves. Enforce that rule, and keep an eye on what gets installed.
requirements.whyItMatters: Software installed without oversight can carry malware or quietly send company data somewhere it shouldn't go.
examples: Employees can't install software themselves; they ask IT for it.
Device management lists the software on each laptop, and new installations are reviewed.
evidence: Software installation policy
Settings that restrict who can install software
Software inventory or installation reports

requirements.text: Identify system users, processes acting on behalf of users, and devices.
requirements.plainEnglish: Give every person, automated program, and device its own unique name or ID in your systems. Then you can always tell who or what did something.
requirements.whyItMatters: Unique IDs make it possible to control access and to trace actions back to a specific person or device.
examples: Each employee has a unique username such as jsmith@yourcompany.com.
Service accounts used by backup software are named and documented.
Company laptops are registered in a device management tool by name or serial number.
evidence: User account list showing unique IDs
Inventory of devices and service accounts
Identification and authentication policy

requirements.text: Authenticate (or verify) the identities of users, processes, or devices, as a prerequisite to allowing access to organizational systems.
requirements.plainEnglish: Before anyone or anything gets in, make them prove they are who they say they are. Usually that means a password plus something else, or a certificate for devices.
requirements.whyItMatters: A username alone is easy to guess. Verifying identity stops people from simply claiming to be someone else.
examples: Users must enter a password to sign in to their computer and email.
Devices must be enrolled in device management before they can reach company files.
evidence: Authentication settings screenshots
Identification and authentication policy
Device enrollment or certificate configuration

requirements.text: Use multifactor authentication for local and network access to privileged accounts and for network access to non-privileged accounts.
requirements.plainEnglish: Require a second step beyond a password, such as a code from a phone app or a security key. This is called multifactor authentication (MFA). Admin accounts need it everywhere. Regular accounts need it whenever they connect over a network, such as signing in to cloud email or a VPN (a secure connection into the company network).
requirements.whyItMatters: Stolen passwords are one of the most common ways attackers get in. A second factor stops most of those attempts.
examples: All Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace accounts require an authenticator app at sign-in.
Admin accounts require a hardware security key, even when signing in at the office.
evidence: MFA configuration screenshots
Report showing MFA enrollment status for all users
Identification and authentication policy

requirements.text: Employ replay-resistant authentication mechanisms for network access to privileged and non-privileged accounts.
requirements.plainEnglish: Use sign-in methods that can't be fooled by an attacker who records a sign-in and plays it back later. Modern multifactor authentication (MFA) with one-time codes or security keys, and sign-ins over encrypted connections, are designed to resist this.
requirements.whyItMatters: If a recorded sign-in could be reused, an attacker who captured it once could sign in as that person again.
examples: Network sign-ins use modern, encrypted sign-in methods, and older methods that send reusable passwords are turned off.
MFA uses one-time codes or security keys, which can't be reused.
evidence: Documentation of the sign-in methods your systems use
Settings showing older, replayable sign-in methods are turned off

requirements.text: Prevent reuse of identifiers for a defined period.
requirements.plainEnglish: Don't give a username that belonged to someone else to a new person until a set period has passed. Decide how long that period is.
requirements.whyItMatters: If a new person gets an old username right away, permissions, logs, and email from the two people can get mixed up.
examples: Usernames of former employees aren't reassigned for two years.
A new employee with the same name as a former one gets a different username, such as jsmith2.
evidence: Account management policy stating how long a username can't be reused
Account records showing the rule is followed

requirements.text: Disable identifiers after a defined period of inactivity.
requirements.plainEnglish: Disable accounts that haven't been used for a set period, such as 90 days. Decide the period, and make sure your systems or a regular review enforce it.
requirements.whyItMatters: Forgotten accounts are easy targets, because nobody notices when someone else starts using them.
examples: Accounts unused for 90 days are disabled automatically.
A monthly report of inactive accounts is reviewed, and unused accounts are disabled.
evidence: Policy stating the inactivity period
Settings or reports showing inactive accounts are disabled

requirements.text: Enforce a minimum password complexity and change of characters when new passwords are created.
requirements.plainEnglish: Set minimum rules for new passwords, such as a minimum length and a mix of character types. Also require a new password to differ from the old one by a certain number of characters. Write the rules down and set your systems to enforce them.
requirements.whyItMatters: Short or simple passwords can be guessed quickly. Requiring real change stops people from just adding a number to their old password.
examples: New passwords must be at least 14 characters long and include several types of characters.
A new password must change a set number of characters from the previous one, where the system supports this setting.
evidence: Password policy stating the complexity and change rules
Screenshots of password settings in your systems

requirements.text: Prohibit password reuse for a specified number of generations.
requirements.plainEnglish: Don't let people reuse their recent passwords. Decide how many previous passwords are blocked, such as the last 24, and set your systems to enforce it.
requirements.whyItMatters: If people can switch back to an old password, a password that was stolen once can work again.
examples: Systems remember each person's last 24 passwords and won't accept any of them again.
evidence: Password policy stating how many previous passwords are blocked
Screenshots of password history settings

requirements.text: Allow temporary password use for system logons with an immediate change to a permanent password.
requirements.plainEnglish: Sometimes you give someone a temporary password, such as for a new account or a password reset. Make them change it to a password of their own the first time they sign in.
requirements.whyItMatters: Temporary passwords are often sent by email or written down. Forcing a change means only the user knows the real password.
examples: New accounts and password resets are set to require a password change at the next sign-in.
evidence: Account setup and password reset procedure
Settings showing users must change temporary passwords at first sign-in

requirements.text: Store and transmit only cryptographically-protected passwords.
requirements.plainEnglish: Passwords should never be stored or sent in readable form. Systems should store them scrambled in a way that can't be reversed (called hashing) and send them only over encrypted connections.
requirements.whyItMatters: If passwords are stored or sent as plain text, anyone who gets the file or intercepts the traffic gets every password.
examples: Sign-in pages use encrypted connections (HTTPS).
Shared passwords are kept in a password manager, not in spreadsheets or documents.
Any custom application stores passwords hashed, never as plain text.
evidence: Vendor documentation showing passwords are stored hashed and sent encrypted
Policy banning passwords in plain-text files or email

requirements.text: Obscure feedback of authentication information.
requirements.plainEnglish: When someone types a password, show dots or asterisks instead of the actual characters. This is the default on almost all systems, so mainly make sure it hasn't been turned off.
requirements.whyItMatters: Hiding passwords on screen stops people nearby from reading them over the user's shoulder.
examples: Password fields on computers, phones, and sign-in pages show dots instead of characters.
evidence: Screenshots of sign-in screens showing hidden password entry

requirements.text: Establish an operational incident-handling capability for organizational systems that includes preparation, detection, analysis, containment, recovery, and user response activities.
requirements.plainEnglish: Be ready to handle security incidents, such as a hacked email account, ransomware, or a lost laptop with CUI on it. Write a plan that covers getting ready, spotting incidents, working out what happened, stopping the damage, recovering, and what users should do. Make sure the people named in the plan know their roles.
requirements.whyItMatters: When an incident hits, there's no time to work out who to call or what to do. A plan prepared in advance limits the damage and speeds up recovery.
examples: A two-page incident response plan lists who to call, first steps for common incidents, and how to recover from backups.
Employees know to report anything suspicious to a named person right away.
Your contract with your IT provider covers help during incidents.
evidence: Incident response plan
List of incident response roles and contacts
Records of past incidents and how they were handled

requirements.text: Track, document, and report incidents to designated officials and/or authorities both internal and external to the organization.
requirements.plainEnglish: Keep a record of each security incident: what happened, when, what you did, and how it ended. Decide who inside the company must be told and which outside authorities must be notified, and then notify them. Defense contracts often require reporting certain cyber incidents within a set time, so check your contract.
requirements.whyItMatters: A written record helps you learn from incidents and shows what you did. Some reports are required by your contracts, and reporting late can cause problems with your customer.
examples: An incident log records each incident, the actions taken, and who was notified.

If your contract includes clause 252.204-7012 of the DFARS (the Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement), cyber incidents affecting covered defense information must be reported to the Department of Defense within 72 hours.
The plan names who inside the company must be told, such as the owner.
evidence: Incident log or tickets
List of internal and external parties to notify, with contact details
Copies of past incident reports

requirements.text: Test the organizational incident response capability.
requirements.plainEnglish: Practice your incident response plan to make sure it works. A simple way is a tabletop exercise: walk through a made-up incident, like ransomware, and talk through who does what. Fix any gaps you find.
requirements.whyItMatters: Plans that are never tested often fail when they're needed, because contacts are out of date or steps don't work.
examples: Once a year, the team walks through a pretend ransomware attack using the plan.
A test restore from backup confirms that recovery works.
evidence: Records of incident response tests or exercises, with dates and participants
Notes on lessons learned and updates made to the plan

requirements.text: Perform maintenance on organizational systems.
requirements.plainEnglish: Keep your systems maintained: install updates, repair or replace failing equipment, and do routine upkeep on schedule. Keep records of the maintenance done.
requirements.whyItMatters: Neglected systems break down and develop security weaknesses. Records show what was done and when.
examples: Your IT provider performs monthly maintenance and logs the work.
Failing hard drives and aging equipment are repaired or replaced on schedule.
evidence: Maintenance procedure or schedule
Maintenance records or tickets

requirements.text: Provide controls on the tools, techniques, mechanisms, and personnel used to conduct system maintenance.
requirements.plainEnglish: Control who does maintenance on your systems and what tools and methods they use. Only approved people and tools should be used, especially remote support software.
requirements.whyItMatters: Maintenance tools and the people who use them often have powerful access. If they're not controlled, they can be misused or bring in malware.
examples: Only the approved IT provider and named staff may perform maintenance.
Only approved remote support tools are allowed, and others are blocked.
Maintenance tools are kept up to date and stored securely.
evidence: List of approved maintenance staff and tools
Maintenance policy
Settings that block unapproved remote support tools

requirements.text: Ensure equipment removed for off-site maintenance is sanitized of any CUI.
requirements.plainEnglish: Before sending equipment out for repair, remove any CUI from it. For example, wipe or remove the hard drive before a laptop goes back to the manufacturer.
requirements.whyItMatters: Repair shops are outside your control. CUI left on a device could be seen by people with no right to see it.
examples: Hard drives are removed or securely wiped before laptops are sent for repair.
A checklist for off-site repairs includes removing or wiping storage.
evidence: Procedure for preparing equipment for off-site repair
Records showing equipment was wiped or its drive removed before it left

requirements.text: Check media containing diagnostic and test programs for malicious code before the media are used in organizational systems.
requirements.plainEnglish: Scan USB drives, discs, or downloads that contain diagnostic or repair tools for malware before using them on your systems. This includes tools a visiting technician brings in.
requirements.whyItMatters: Maintenance tools run with powerful access, so infected tools can spread malware deep into your systems.
examples: Technicians' USB drives are scanned with antivirus software before use.
Diagnostic software is downloaded only from the vendor's official website.
evidence: Maintenance procedure requiring malware scans of diagnostic media
Antivirus scan logs

requirements.text: Require multifactor authentication to establish nonlocal maintenance sessions via external network connections and terminate such connections when nonlocal maintenance is complete.
requirements.plainEnglish: When someone maintains your systems remotely over the internet (called nonlocal maintenance), require multifactor authentication (MFA) to start the session. End the connection as soon as the work is done.
requirements.whyItMatters: Remote maintenance access is a favorite target for attackers. MFA and promptly closed sessions limit the chance it's misused.
examples: Your IT provider's remote support tool requires MFA for its technicians.
Remote sessions are ended, and unattended access is turned off, when the work is complete.
evidence: Remote maintenance tool settings showing MFA is required
Logs showing when sessions start and end
Remote maintenance procedure

requirements.text: Supervise the maintenance activities of maintenance personnel without required access authorization.
requirements.plainEnglish: Some maintenance people don't have approved access to your systems, such as a visiting technician. An employee with approved access should supervise their work.
requirements.whyItMatters: Outsiders working on your systems without supervision could access CUI or make unapproved changes.
examples: An employee stays with the copier technician during repairs.
Visiting maintenance staff are escorted, and their visits are logged.
evidence: Procedure for supervising outside maintenance staff
Visitor or maintenance logs

requirements.text: Protect (i.e., physically control and securely store) system media containing CUI, both paper and digital.
requirements.plainEnglish: Keep paper documents and digital storage that contain CUI under control and stored securely. Digital storage includes USB drives, external hard drives, and backup disks. For example, lock them in a cabinet or a room with limited access.
requirements.whyItMatters: Paper and portable storage are easy to lose, steal, or read. Keeping them under control stops CUI from walking out the door.
examples: Paper documents with CUI are kept in a locked cabinet when not in use.
Backup drives containing CUI are stored in a locked room.
A clean desk rule: CUI isn't left out when people step away.
evidence: Media protection policy
Photos or descriptions of secure storage
Clean desk policy

requirements.text: Limit access to CUI on system media to authorized users.
requirements.plainEnglish: Only people authorized to see CUI should be able to get to the paper or digital media that holds it.
requirements.whyItMatters: Even locked storage doesn't help if too many people have the key.
examples: Only the project team has keys to the CUI file cabinet.
Encrypted USB drives with CUI require a password that only authorized people know.
evidence: List of people authorized to access CUI media
Key or access logs

requirements.text: Sanitize or destroy system media containing CUI before disposal or release for reuse.
requirements.plainEnglish: Before throwing away or reusing anything that held CUI, wipe it so the data can't be recovered, or destroy it. That includes paper, hard drives, USB drives, phones, and copiers with internal storage.
requirements.whyItMatters: Deleted files can often be recovered. Old equipment and paper in the trash are common sources of data leaks.
examples: Paper with CUI goes in a locked shred bin that a shredding service empties.
Old hard drives are destroyed or securely wiped, and the vendor provides a certificate of destruction.
Leased copiers have their storage wiped before they're returned.
evidence: Media sanitization and disposal procedure
Certificates of destruction or records of wiping

requirements.text: Mark media with necessary CUI markings and distribution limitations.
requirements.plainEnglish: Label paper documents and digital media that contain CUI with the required CUI markings and any limits on who may receive them. Your contract and your customer's CUI instructions say which markings to use.
requirements.whyItMatters: Markings tell everyone who handles the material that it needs protection and who may see it.
examples: Documents with CUI carry a CUI banner at the top of each page, as your customer instructs.
USB drives with CUI are labeled as CUI.
evidence: Marking procedure
Examples of marked documents and media

requirements.text: Control access to media containing CUI and maintain accountability for media during transport outside of controlled areas.
requirements.plainEnglish: When CUI on paper or digital media leaves your controlled areas, such as being shipped or carried to a customer, control who handles it. Keep track of it along the way.
requirements.whyItMatters: Media in transit is easy to lose or intercept. Tracking it means you'll know if something goes missing.
examples: CUI is shipped by a tracked carrier, with a signature required.
A log records media that leaves the office, who took it, and when it came back.
evidence: Media transport procedure
Transport logs or shipping records

requirements.text: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of CUI stored on digital media during transport unless otherwise protected by alternative physical safeguards.
requirements.plainEnglish: Encrypt CUI on USB drives, laptops, or other digital media when it's carried or shipped outside your controlled areas. The exception is when it's protected physically in another way, such as a locked container carried by a trusted courier. When encryption protects CUI, it generally needs to be FIPS-validated, meaning tested and approved under a U.S. government standard. Requirement 3.13.11 covers this.
requirements.whyItMatters: Encrypted media that's lost or stolen in transit can't be read.
examples: Only encrypted USB drives may be used to carry CUI.
Laptops have full-disk encryption turned on before they leave the office.
evidence: Encryption policy for media in transport
Records showing encrypted devices are used

requirements.text: Control the use of removable media on system components.
requirements.plainEnglish: Control the use of removable media, such as USB drives, memory cards, and external hard drives, on your computers and other equipment. For example, block them entirely, or allow only approved, encrypted devices.
requirements.whyItMatters: Removable media can carry malware in, or carry CUI out, without anyone noticing.
examples: USB storage is blocked on company computers, except for approved encrypted drives.
Device management settings control which removable devices can be used.
evidence: Removable media policy
Device control settings

requirements.text: Prohibit the use of portable storage devices when such devices have no identifiable owner.
requirements.plainEnglish: Don't allow USB drives or other portable storage that has no known owner. Examples are a drive found in the parking lot or one handed out at a trade show.
requirements.whyItMatters: Attackers sometimes leave infected USB drives where people will find them and plug them in.
examples: Employees are trained to hand found USB drives to IT instead of plugging them in.
Company USB drives are labeled and assigned to named people.
evidence: Policy banning portable storage with no known owner
Training materials covering found devices
List of assigned portable storage devices

requirements.text: Protect the confidentiality of backup CUI at storage locations.
requirements.plainEnglish: Protect backups that contain CUI as carefully as the original data, wherever they're stored. Usually this means encrypting backups and limiting who can access them.
requirements.whyItMatters: Backups hold copies of everything. A poorly protected backup is an easy way to steal all your CUI at once.
examples: Cloud backups are encrypted, and only two admins can access them.
Backup drives stored off-site are encrypted and kept in a locked location.
evidence: Backup policy
Backup settings showing encryption is on
List of people with access to backups

requirements.text: Screen individuals prior to authorizing access to organizational systems containing CUI.
requirements.plainEnglish: Check people out before you give them access to systems that hold Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI). This usually means a background check appropriate for the role.
requirements.whyItMatters: Screening lowers the risk of giving sensitive information to someone who shouldn't have it.
examples: New hires complete a background check before their accounts are created.
Contractors who need system access are screened under the same process as employees.
evidence: Personnel screening policy
Records showing screening was completed before access was granted (without storing sensitive personal details in this tool)

requirements.text: Ensure that organizational systems containing CUI are protected during and after personnel actions such as terminations and transfers.
requirements.plainEnglish: When someone leaves or changes jobs, promptly remove or adjust their access and get back company equipment.
requirements.whyItMatters: Former employees with working accounts are a common and avoidable risk.
examples: An offboarding checklist disables accounts, collects laptops and badges, and changes shared passwords.
When an employee moves to a new role, access they no longer need is removed.
evidence: Offboarding and transfer procedure
Completed offboarding checklists
Account logs showing timely deactivation

requirements.text: Limit physical access to organizational systems, equipment, and the respective operating environments to authorized individuals.
requirements.plainEnglish: Only authorized people should be able to physically get to your computers, servers, network equipment, and the rooms they're in. Keep a list of who is allowed, and use locks, keys, or badges to keep everyone else out.
requirements.whyItMatters: Someone with physical access can steal equipment, plug in a malicious device, or read CUI off a screen.
examples: The server and network equipment are in a locked closet.
Office doors are locked, and only employees have keys or badges.
The list of people with keys is reviewed whenever someone leaves.
evidence: List of people authorized for physical access
Description or photos of locks and secure areas
Key or badge records

requirements.text: Protect and monitor the physical facility and support infrastructure for organizational systems.
requirements.plainEnglish: Protect and keep watch over your office and the things your systems depend on, such as power, cooling, and network cabling. Common measures include locks, alarms, and security cameras.
requirements.whyItMatters: Break-ins, power failures, and tampering with cables can expose CUI or knock your systems offline.
examples: The office alarm system is monitored after hours.
Security cameras cover the entrances and the equipment room.
Network cables and equipment can't be reached from public areas.
evidence: Description of physical security measures
Alarm and camera system records
Facility security procedures

requirements.text: Escort visitors and monitor visitor activity.
requirements.plainEnglish: Escort visitors while they're in areas with your systems or CUI, and keep track of what they do there.
requirements.whyItMatters: Visitors left alone could see CUI, take something, or plug in a device without anyone noticing.
examples: Visitors sign in at the front desk and are escorted by an employee at all times.
Visitors wear visitor badges so they stand out.
evidence: Visitor policy
Visitor sign-in log

requirements.text: Maintain audit logs of physical access.
requirements.plainEnglish: Keep records of who enters your office and secure areas, and when. This can be a badge system's logs or a paper sign-in sheet.
requirements.whyItMatters: Physical access records help you find out who was present if something goes missing or an incident happens.
examples: The badge system records every door entry.
Visitors and after-hours entries are recorded in a sign-in book that is kept for a year.
evidence: Badge system logs
Visitor and entry logs
Policy for how long access records are kept

requirements.text: Control and manage physical access devices.
requirements.plainEnglish: Keep track of physical access devices, such as keys, key cards, badges, and door codes. Know who has each one, collect them when people leave, and change locks or codes when needed.
requirements.whyItMatters: Lost keys or badges, or door codes that never change, let in people who shouldn't be there.
examples: A key log lists every key and who holds it.
Badges are deactivated and keys collected on an employee's last day.
Door codes are changed when someone leaves.
evidence: Inventory of keys, badges, and codes, and who holds each
Records of keys collected and badges deactivated

requirements.text: Enforce safeguarding measures for CUI at alternate work sites.
requirements.plainEnglish: Set rules for protecting CUI when people work somewhere other than the office, such as at home or while traveling. Make sure the rules are followed.
requirements.whyItMatters: Home offices and public places don't have the office's locks and controls. Clear rules help keep CUI safe there.
examples: Remote workers must use company laptops, lock their screens, and keep CUI out of view of family members and the public.
CUI may not be printed at home.
Remote workers sign that they've read the remote work rules.
evidence: Remote work security policy
Signed acknowledgments from remote workers

requirements.text: Periodically assess the risk to organizational operations (including mission, functions, image, or reputation), organizational assets, and individuals, resulting from the operation of organizational systems and the associated processing, storage, or transmission of CUI.
requirements.plainEnglish: Regularly assess the security risks to your business from the systems that handle CUI. Think about what could go wrong, how likely it is, and how bad it would be. Decide how often you'll do this, such as once a year.
requirements.whyItMatters: You can't protect against everything at once. A risk assessment shows where to focus your time and money.
examples: Once a year, the owner and IT provider list threats such as ransomware, lost laptops, and phishing, and rate how likely and how harmful each one is.
The risk assessment is updated after major changes, such as moving to a new cloud service.
evidence: Risk assessment document, with the date it was done
Policy stating how often risk is assessed

requirements.text: Scan for vulnerabilities in organizational systems and applications periodically and when new vulnerabilities affecting those systems and applications are identified.
requirements.plainEnglish: Scan your systems and applications for known security weaknesses, called vulnerabilities, on a regular schedule. Also scan when new weaknesses are announced that could affect you. Decide how often you'll scan.
requirements.whyItMatters: Attackers use automated tools to find known weaknesses. Scanning lets you find and fix them first.
examples: A vulnerability scanning tool checks all computers and servers every month.
When a major new vulnerability is announced, an extra scan checks whether you're affected.
Your IT provider runs the scans and sends you the reports.
evidence: Vulnerability scanning policy stating how often scans run
Scan reports

requirements.text: Remediate vulnerabilities in accordance with risk assessments.
requirements.plainEnglish: Fix the weaknesses you find, starting with the most serious, based on your risk assessment. Track each one until it's fixed or a decision is made about it.
requirements.whyItMatters: Finding weaknesses doesn't help unless you fix them. Prioritizing by risk puts the dangerous ones first.
examples: Critical vulnerabilities are fixed within 15 days and others within 30 days, as your policy sets.
Vulnerabilities that can't be fixed yet are tracked in your plan of action with a target date.
evidence: Vulnerability fix records or tickets
Policy with time frames for fixing vulnerabilities
Follow-up scan reports showing the fixes worked
